solution.trap: Reading 'randomised' as 'no worst case'. A randomised quicksort still has a Θ(n²) worst case for a particular unlucky sequence of pivots; what disappears is the fixed adversarial input.

questions.question: Two sorted runs of 5 and 8 keys are merged by the standard two-way merge. What is the largest number of key comparisons the merge can perform? (Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: A two-way merge compares the two current heads and outputs the smaller one, so every comparison removes exactly one key except the last, when one run is already exhausted.
steps: Each comparison consumes one key from one of the two runs.
The merge ends as soon as one run is empty; the remaining keys of the other run are copied without any comparison.
The worst case leaves exactly one key in a run when the other is exhausted, so the number of comparisons is at most m + n − 1.
solution.trap: Answering 13 by adding the run lengths, or 8 by assuming the longer run is scanned completely. The minimum is 5, reached when every key of the shorter run is smaller than every key of the longer one.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the comparison count of quicksort are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: On a uniformly random permutation the expected number of comparisons is 2n ln n + O(n), about 1.39 n log₂ n.
If every partition splits off exactly one element, then T(n) = T(n−1) + Θ(n) gives T(n) = Θ(n²).
That same one-sided recurrence gives a recursion depth of Θ(log n).
If every partition splits the array in the ratio 1 : 9, then T(n) = T(n/10) + T(9n/10) + Θ(n) is Θ(n log n).

solution.concept: A quicksort recurrence is governed by how much of the array the two recursive calls still cover: a constant fraction below 1 keeps the level cost Θ(n) and the depth Θ(log n).
steps: (A) The expected comparison count is Σₖ₋ₖ 2/(j−i+1) over all pairs, which evaluates to 2n ln n + O(n); converting to base 2 gives the factor 2/ln 2 ≈ 1.39. TRUE.
(C) The same recurrence removes one element per level, so its depth is n, not log n. FALSE.
(D) The level cost is at most n and the depth is log₁₀/₉ n = Θ(log n), so the total is Θ(n log n); the constant factor is about 1/log₂(10/9) ≈ 6.6. TRUE.
solution.trap: Assuming any unbalanced split is quadratic. Only a split that removes a constant number of elements per level is quadratic; a fixed ratio such as 1 : 9 still leaves a constant fraction to recurse on.

questions.question: Quicksort uses the Lomuto partition with the last element as pivot. Its loop performs the exchange a[i] ↔ a[j] every time a[j] ≤ pivot, even when i = j, and one final exchange places the pivot. Run on the whole array [7, 3, 9, 4, 2, 8, 5], how many exchanges does the complete quicksort perform in total? (Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: The exchange count of a Lomuto quicksort is a trace, not a formula: every partition must be followed by hand, and self-exchanges count because the code executes them.
steps: First partition, pivot 5: 3 and 4 and 2 are moved (3 exchanges) and the pivot is placed (1), giving [3, 4, 2, 5, 9, 8, 7] with the pivot at index 4 (1-based). Total so far 4.
Left part [3, 4, 2], pivot 2: no key is ≤ 2, so the only exchange is the final one, giving [2, 4, 3]. Total 5.
Left part [4, 3], pivot 3: no key is ≤ 3, so again only the final exchange, giving [2, 3, 4]. Total 6.
Right part [9, 8, 7], pivot 7: no key is ≤ 7, so only the final exchange, giving [7, 8, 9]. Total 7.
Right part [8, 9], pivot 9: 8 ≤ 9 causes a self-exchange a[i] ↔ a[i] (1) and the final exchange is also a self-exchange (1). Total 9.
The array is now sorted and no further call has more than one element.
solution.trap: Reporting 7 by skipping the two self-exchanges in the last partition. In Lomuto's loop the exchange is executed whenever a[j] ≤ pivot, whether or not i = j, and the final exchange is executed even when the pivot is already in place - the question fixes that convention precisely so the count is unambiguous.

questions.question: Which of the following does counting sort NOT use?
options: A count array of size k for keys in the range 0..k−1.
A comparison between two keys.
A prefix-sum pass over the count array.
A stable placement pass over the input.

solution.concept: Counting sort indexes an array by key value instead of deciding order by comparing keys, which is why it escapes the Ω(n log n) comparison lower bound.
steps: Counting sort builds C[v] = number of keys equal to v for v in 0..k−1; this uses a count array of size k.
A prefix sum turns C[v] into the number of keys ≤ v, which gives every key its final position.
Placing the keys from right to left makes the pass stable.
No step ever compares two keys with each other.
solution.trap: Believing every sort must compare. Only comparison sorts are bound by Ω(n log n); counting sort trades a Θ(k) array for the right to avoid comparisons.

questions.question: n = 500 keys, each an integer in the range 0..999 999, must be sorted. Counting sort runs in Θ(n + k). Why is it a poor choice here?
options: The 10⁶-entry count array dominates the cost, so the running time is Θ(k) = Θ(10⁶) rather than Θ(n).
Counting sort requires all keys to be distinct.
Counting sort is unstable when the key range is large.
Counting sort cannot handle keys above 65 535.

solution.concept: Counting sort pays for the size of the key universe, not only for the number of keys.
steps: The count array of 10⁶ entries must be zeroed and then prefix-summed, which costs more than a comparison sort of 500 keys by many orders of magnitude.
Distinctness is not required - the prefix sum handles duplicates.
Stability does not depend on the key range, and there is no 16-bit limit in the algorithm.
solution.trap: Quoting Θ(n + k) as if it were Θ(n). The k term is the whole point: a sparse, wide key range makes counting sort arbitrarily bad.

questions.question: n keys, each an integer in the range 1..n², must be sorted. Which method runs in Θ(n) time?
options: Any comparison sort, because the keys are integers.
Counting sort with a count array of size n².
Radix sort with base n, which needs only two digit passes.
Quicksort with a median-of-three pivot.

solution.concept: Radix sort in base b costs Θ(d(n + b)) with d = ⌈log_b M⌉; choosing b ≈ n makes the per-pass cost Θ(n) and the pass count a constant.
steps: The keys are below n², so in base n each key has d = ⌈log_n n²⌉ = 2 digits.
Each pass is a stable counting sort over n + 1 buckets, costing Θ(n + n) = Θ(n).
Two passes give Θ(2n) = Θ(n).
Counting sort alone would need a count array of size n², costing Θ(n²), and any comparison sort costs Ω(n log n).
solution.trap: Choosing counting sort because the keys are small integers - they are small only relative to n², which is far too wide. The comparison lower bound also applies to integer keys unless a non-comparison method is used.

questions.question: LSD radix sort with base b is applied to n keys whose largest value is M. It performs d = ⌈log_b M⌉ passes, each costing Θ(n + b). Which base minimises the total cost Θ(d(n + b))?
options: b = 2, because each pass is then as cheap as possible.
b ≈ n, which balances the per-pass cost n + b against the number of passes.
b = M, because a single pass then suffices.
b = n², because the count array then fits in cache.

solution.concept: The total cost d(n + b) = (ln M / ln b)(n + b) trades the number of passes against the width of each pass's count array.
steps: Write the cost as C(b) = (ln M / ln b)(n + b).
For b much smaller than n the term n + b ≈ n, but d grows like ln M / ln b - too many passes.
For b much larger than n the pass count shrinks slowly while each pass pays Θ(b) - too wide a count array.
The minimum of C(b) sits near b = n; at that point d = log_n M and the cost is Θ(n log_n M).
b = M gives one pass but a count array of M entries, which is exactly the counting sort cost the radix trick was meant to avoid.
solution.trap: Maximising the base to minimise the passes. One pass with a count array of size M is counting sort, whose cost is Θ(M) and can dwarf Θ(n).

questions.question: Which of the following statements about radix sort are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: LSD radix sort is a stable sort of the whole keys.
It compares keys in pairs, so it cannot beat the Ω(n log n) bound.
With base b and d-digit keys its running time is Θ(d(n + b)).
When every key is equal, LSD radix sort still performs all d passes.

solution.concept: LSD radix sort is a sequence of stable passes, one per digit, from the least significant digit to the most significant.
steps: (A) Each pass is stable and the passes run from the least significant digit upwards, so keys that agree on all digits keep their original relative order. TRUE.
(B) Radix sort never compares two keys; it distributes them into buckets by digit. FALSE - it is a non-comparison sort and is not bound by Ω(n log n).
(C) d passes, each a stable counting sort over b + 1 buckets on n keys, cost Θ(d(n + b)). TRUE.
(D) The pass count depends only on the number of digits, not on the values, so equal keys still go through d passes. TRUE.
solution.trap: Assuming that because radix sort is 'linear' it must be a comparison sort with a loophole, or that it can stop early when the data look sorted. Neither is true: the pass count is fixed by the key width.

questions.question: LSD radix sort with base 16 is applied to 32-bit unsigned integers. How many passes does it need? (Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Each base-16 pass consumes four bits, so the number of passes is the bit width divided by the digits' width in bits.
steps: A base-16 digit encodes log₂ 16 = 4 bits.
A 32-bit key therefore has 32 / 4 = 8 digits in base 16.
LSD radix sort performs one pass per digit.
So the pass count is 8, and each pass uses a count array of 17 slots (0..15 plus the prefix-sum slot).
solution.trap: Answering 16 by using the number of symbols in the base rather than the number of bits per symbol, or 32 by forgetting that each pass handles four bits at once.

questions.question: Quickselect looks for the 3rd smallest key of 100 distinct keys. Its first partition returns a pivot that is the 40th smallest. Which part does the algorithm recurse into?
options: The part holding the 39 keys smaller than the pivot.
The part holding the 60 keys larger than the pivot.
Both parts, because both are still needed.
Neither; the answer is the pivot itself.

solution.concept: A partition tells you the exact rank of the pivot, so it also tells you on which side of it the wanted rank must lie.
steps: The pivot is the 40th smallest, so the 39 keys to its left are the 1st to 39th smallest.
The target rank 3 is among them, so the answer lies in the left part.
The right part holds ranks 41 to 100 and cannot contain rank 3, so it is discarded.
Only one side is recursed into, which is what makes quickselect Θ(n) in expectation rather than Θ(n log n).
solution.trap: Recursing into both parts, which turns quickselect back into quicksort. The single-sided recursion is the whole reason selection is cheaper than sorting.

questions.question: Finding the maximum of n distinct keys needs at least n − 1 comparisons. Which argument proves this?
options: The maximum must be compared with every other key, so n comparisons are needed.
Sorting the array first is necessary, which costs Ω(n log n).
The maximum can be found only by a tournament of depth log₂ n.
Every key except the maximum must lose at least one comparison, and one comparison produces at most one loser.

solution.concept: An adversary argument: a key that has never lost a comparison could still be the maximum, so the algorithm cannot stop before n − 1 keys have lost.
steps: A comparison between two keys makes exactly one of them a loser.
If some key other than the true maximum has never lost, then swapping it with the maximum gives an input consistent with every comparison seen so far but with a different answer.
So an algorithm that has performed fewer than n − 1 comparisons cannot be correct.
n − 1 comparisons suffice, by scanning and keeping the current maximum.
solution.trap: Option (A) is the intuitive but wrong count: the maximum is not compared with itself, so n − 1 comparisons are enough, not n.

questions.question: Which is the correct lower bound for finding the median of n distinct keys?
options: Ω(n log n), because the median is a special case of sorting.
Ω(log n), because a binary search over the ranks suffices.
Ω(n), because every key must be inspected at least once, and Ω(n) is achievable.
Ω(1), because the median of a sorted array sits at a fixed index.

solution.concept: A lower bound applies to a problem, not to the method used to solve it: selection is strictly weaker than sorting, so sorting's bound does not transfer.
steps: Any correct algorithm must read every key, since an unread key could be the median; that gives the Ω(n) bound.
Median-of-medians finds the median in Θ(n) worst-case time, so the bound is tight.
Sorting is one way to find the median, but it is not the only way, and a harder problem's bound does not constrain an easier one.
The Ω(n log n) bound applies to producing the whole sorted order, which selection does not need.
solution.trap: Assuming that because the median can be found by sorting, the sorting bound must apply. Reductions give upper bounds on difficulty in one direction only.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the median-of-medians (BFPRT) selection algorithm are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Grouping into blocks of 3 keeps the same guarantee, because a constant block size is all that matters.
With groups of 5 it guarantees that at least 3n/10 − 6 keys are no larger than the chosen pivot and at least 3n/10 − 6 are no smaller.
Its worst-case running time obeys T(n) ≤ T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + Θ(n), which solves to Θ(n).
It chooses its pivot deterministically, without randomisation.

solution.concept: A deterministic pivot is good enough when it is guaranteed to discard a constant fraction, so that the two recursive calls together cover less than the whole array.
steps: (B) Half of the ⌈n/5⌉ block medians are at most the median of medians, and each such median has three block elements at most itself; discounting the pivot's own block and the last, incomplete block leaves at least 3n/10 − 6 keys on each side. TRUE.
(C) One call of size n/5 chooses the pivot, and at most 7n/10 keys remain to be searched; since 1/5 + 7/10 = 9/10 < 1, the total is Θ(n). TRUE.
(A) Blocks of 3 give the recurrence T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + Θ(n), and 1/3 + 2/3 = 1, which solves to Θ(n log n) rather than Θ(n). FALSE - the constant 5 matters, not merely constancy.
(D) The pivot is the median of the block medians, computed recursively; there is no random choice. TRUE.
solution.trap: Thinking any constant block size works. The sum of the two recursion fractions must be strictly below 1; with blocks of 3 it equals 1 and the linear bound collapses.

questions.question: The median-of-medians algorithm with groups of 5 processes n = 60 keys. Using the standard guarantee 3n/10 − 6, at least how many keys are guaranteed to be no smaller than the chosen pivot? (Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: The pivot of median-of-medians is the median of the block medians, so half the blocks contribute three keys at least as large as it.
steps: The guarantee is 3n/10 − 6 keys on each side of the pivot.
Subtract 6 to discount the pivot's own block and the incomplete last block: 18 − 6 = 12.
So at least 12 keys are ≥ the pivot and at least 12 are ≤ it, which is what bounds the recursive call at 7n/10.
solution.trap: Forgetting the −6 correction and answering 18. The correction accounts for the block containing the pivot and the block that may be short.

questions.question: Why does the recurrence T(n) ≤ T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + Θ(n) of median-of-medians solve to Θ(n)?
options: Because 1/5 + 7/10 = 9/10 < 1, so the work per level forms a geometric series with ratio below 1.
Because T(n/5) is asymptotically negligible beside T(7n/10) and can be dropped.
Because 7n/10 < n for every n, so the recursion must terminate.
Because the pivot is chosen at random, so the expected split is balanced.

solution.concept: For a recurrence whose recursive subproblem sizes sum to a fraction c < 1 of n, the total work is bounded by a geometric series and stays Θ(n).
steps: Level 1 costs at most cn for a constant c.
Level 2 costs at most c(n/5 + 7n/10) = c(9n/10).
Level k costs at most c(9/10)^(k−1) n.
Summing the geometric series gives cn / (1 − 9/10) = 10cn = Θ(n).
The recursion depth is log₁₀/₉ n = Θ(log n), but each level is smaller by a constant factor, so the depth does not add a log factor to the total.
solution.trap: Option (C) is the usual confusion: termination only gives an upper bound of n levels times Θ(n) per level, that is Θ(n²), or Θ(n log n) if the levels shrink slowly. The constant ratio below 1 is what turns it linear.

questions.question: A permutation of n distinct keys has inversion count I. Its reverse - the same keys read backwards - has inversion count I′. What is I + I′?
options: n(n − 1)/4, for every permutation
n(n − 1)/2, for every permutation
n², for every permutation
It depends on the permutation

solution.concept: Reversing an array reverses the left-to-right order of every pair, so exactly one of the two orders of each pair is an inversion.
steps: Take any two positions p < q in the original array, holding values x and y.
In the reversed array the same two values appear in the opposite order: y before x.
So the pair {x, y} contributes an inversion in exactly one of the two arrays.
There are n(n − 1)/2 pairs, hence I + I′ = n(n − 1)/2.
Check with n = 3 and a = [1, 2, 3]: I = 0, the reverse is [3, 2, 1] with I′ = 3, and 3 = 3 × 2 / 2.
solution.trap: Assuming the reverse has the same inversion count, or that the sum depends on the permutation. The identity is exact for every permutation.

questions.question: Two adjacent elements of an array are exchanged. What happens to the inversion count?
options: It may change by more than 1.
It never changes, because the multiset of keys is unchanged.
It changes by exactly 1, up or down, and by nothing else.
It changes by exactly n.

solution.concept: An adjacent exchange only reorders one pair; every other pair keeps its relative order.
steps: Let the exchanged neighbours hold x at position k and y at position k+1, with x < y before the exchange.
Any other element is either before both or after both, so its relative order with x and with y is unchanged.
The only pair whose order flips is (x, y), which was not an inversion and becomes one.
Hence the count rises by exactly 1; exchanging them back lowers it by exactly 1.
solution.trap: Thinking a swap can fix several inversions at once. Only a non-adjacent exchange can, which is why bubble sort and insertion sort need exactly I adjacent exchanges while a general swap can fix more.

questions.question: An array a[1..n] is a permutation. Let I be its inversion count and let C be the number of cycles of the permutation, a fixed point counting as a cycle. Which statement is TRUE?
options: I = n − C for every permutation.
Both I and n − C equal the minimum number of adjacent exchanges.
I ≤ n − C for every permutation.
I is the minimum number of adjacent exchanges needed to sort a, and n − C is the minimum number of arbitrary exchanges needed to sort it.

solution.concept: Two different distance measures: adjacent exchanges (inversions) and exchanges of any two positions (cycle decomposition).
steps: An adjacent exchange changes the inversion count by exactly 1, and insertion sort achieves the sort with exactly I of them, so I is the adjacent-exchange distance.
An exchange of any two positions can join two cycles or split one, so each exchange reduces the cycle count by at most 1.
A sorted array has n cycles (n fixed points), so at least n − C exchanges are needed, and n − C suffice by fixing one cycle at a time.
The two quantities differ in general: for a = [2, 3, 1] we get I = 2 but C = 1, so n − C = 2; for a = [3, 2, 1] we get I = 3 while C = 2 and n − C = 1.
solution.trap: Equating the two distances. The last example separates them: [3, 2, 1] needs three adjacent exchanges but only one general exchange.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about counting inversions with a modified merge sort are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Every inversion is counted exactly once, at the level of the recursion where the two keys first fall into different halves.
Whenever the current key of the right run is taken, the number of keys still left in the left run is added to the count.
The algorithm needs Θ(n²) time, because an array of n keys has Θ(n²) pairs.
Equal keys never contribute, so the count stays well defined when the array has duplicates.

solution.concept: The merge step sees two sorted runs and can count, in one step, all pairs that cross the split.
steps: (A) A pair is either inside one half, where the recursive calls count it, or split across the two halves, where this merge counts it. The two cases partition all pairs. TRUE.
(B) If the right key is smaller than the left key at position i, then every key from i to the end of the left run is larger, so the whole tail is a set of inversions with this right key. TRUE.
(C) The counting adds Θ(1) work to each merge comparison, so the total remains Θ(n log n). FALSE.
(D) An inversion needs a strictly larger key on the left; equal keys are never counted, so duplicates are handled consistently. TRUE.
solution.trap: Counting inversions twice, once in the merge and once in the recursion, or adding 1 instead of the size of the remaining left run.

questions.question: How many inversions does the array [5, 2, 4, 1, 3, 2, 6, 1] contain, where an inversion is a pair of indices i < j with a[i] > a[j]? (Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Count per position, looking only to the right, and remember that equal keys never form an inversion.
steps: Position 1 (value 5): smaller to its right are 2, 4, 1, 3, 2, 1 - six inversions.
Position 2 (value 2): the two 1s - two inversions.
Position 3 (value 4): 1, 3, 2, 1 - four inversions.
Position 4 (value 1): nothing smaller - zero.
Position 5 (value 3): 2 and 1 - two inversions.
Position 6 (value 2): the 1 - one inversion. Position 7 (value 6): the 1 - one inversion. Position 8 (value 1): zero.
solution.trap: Counting the two 2s against each other, or counting the two 1s against each other. An inversion needs a strictly greater key on the left, so equal values never contribute - the duplicate 1s and 2s are where most miscounts happen.

questions.question: For a permutation a[1..n] define the inversion vector d_i = #{ j > i : a[j] < a[i] }. Which statement is TRUE?
options: 0 ≤ d_i ≤ n − i for each i, the sum of the d_i is the inversion count, and the map from permutations to inversion vectors is a bijection.
0 ≤ d_i ≤ n − 1 for each i, and the map from permutations to inversion vectors is a bijection.
The sum of the d_i equals n(n − 1)/2 for every permutation.
The inversion vector determines only the parity of the permutation.

solution.concept: The inversion vector (Lehmer code) records, for each position, how many smaller keys lie to its right; its ranges are independent, which makes it a bijection.
steps: d_i counts keys to the right of position i, and there are only n − i of them, so 0 ≤ d_i ≤ n − i.
Summing d_i over all i counts every inversion exactly once, at its left endpoint.
The number of possible vectors is the product over i of (n − i + 1) = n!, which equals the number of permutations.
The reconstruction is constructive - insert keys from the largest down, placing the key of rank k at the position fixed by its d value - so distinct permutations give distinct vectors.
The sum is n(n−1)/2 only for the decreasing permutation, not for every one, and the vector determines the whole permutation, not just its parity.
solution.trap: Option (B) replaces the position-dependent bound n − i by the uniform n − 1, which would allow n^n vectors instead of n! and destroy the bijection.

questions.question: In the fractional knapsack problem the items are divisible, so any fraction of an item may be taken. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: Taking items in decreasing order of value, and then the remainder of the next item, is optimal.
Taking items in decreasing order of value per unit weight, and then the remainder of the next item, is optimal; the same rule can be suboptimal for 0/1 knapsack.
Taking items in increasing order of weight is optimal, and the same rule is also optimal for 0/1 knapsack.
Fractional knapsack is NP-hard, so no polynomial-time algorithm is known for it.

solution.concept: The exchange rate between weight and value is the ratio v_i/w_i. When weight is divisible, the only thing that matters is which item gives the most value per unit of the scarce resource, so the greedy rule sorts by ratio.
steps: Fractional knapsack is a linear program whose feasible region is a simplex-like polytope; its extreme points take all items in ratio order and at most one item fractionally.
Hence sorting by decreasing v_i/w_i and filling the knapsack in that order is optimal (option B).
Sorting by value alone ignores weight: a light item of moderate value can beat a heavy item of slightly larger value, so option A fails.

Sorting by weight ignores value altogether, and for 0/1 knapsack even the ratio rule fails — for example capacity 10 with items (6, 30), (5, 20), (5, 20): ratio-greedy returns 30 while taking both 5-weight items gives 40.
Fractional knapsack is solved in O(n log n) by the ratio rule, so it is not NP-hard; 0/1 knapsack is the NP-hard relative.
solution.trap: Believing that the ratio rule is optimal for both variants. Divisibility is exactly what makes the exchange argument work; with indivisible items the leftover capacity can make the greedy answer worse than optimal.

questions.question: A knapsack has capacity 15. Three items are available, given as (weight, value): (10, 60), (5, 25) and (10, 40). Items may be split. What value does the ratio-greedy algorithm obtain?

solution.concept: Ratio-greedy orders items by value per unit weight, takes whole items while they fit and then the largest fraction of the next item that still fits.
steps: Order: item 1 (ratio 6), item 2 (ratio 5), item 3 (ratio 4).
Take item 1 whole: weight 10, value 60, capacity left 5.
Take item 2 whole: weight 5, value 25, capacity left 0.
Total value = 60 + 25 = 85; item 3 contributes nothing.
solution.trap: Adding the two largest values, 60 + 40 = 100, and stopping because the capacity is exhausted. Those two items weigh 10 + 10 = 20, more than the capacity 15, so the answer is infeasible. Check the weight, not the value, while filling.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about fractional knapsack and its greedy algorithm are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: The greedy algorithm that considers items in decreasing order of value per unit weight is optimal.
In an optimal solution produced by the ratio rule, at most one item is taken fractionally.
The greedy algorithm is asymptotically slower than the pseudo-polynomial dynamic program for 0/1 knapsack, so the dynamic program is preferred for large capacities.
If every item has the same weight, sorting by decreasing value gives an optimal solution.
The linear-programming relaxation of fractional knapsack always has an integral optimal solution.

solution.concept: The ratio rule fills the knapsack in one pass over the ratio-sorted order, so all items before the break point are whole and all after it are zero — only the break item can be partial.
steps: (A) is the optimality theorem for fractional knapsack.
(B) holds because a single item straddles the capacity boundary; every earlier item fits entirely and every later item does not fit at all.
(C) is false: the ratio rule is O(n log n), while the 0/1 dynamic program is O(nC), which is pseudo-polynomial and slower for large C.
(D) is true: with equal weights, v_i/w_i = v_i/w is a positive multiple of v_i, so ratio order is value order and the same argument applies.
(E) is false: the LP optimum is usually fractional — that is precisely what allows splitting — and is generally not integral.
solution.trap: Confusing the LP relaxation with the integer problem. The relaxation is exactly the fractional problem, and its optimum normally uses a fraction of one item.

questions.question: A knapsack has capacity 20. The available items, given as (weight, value), are (8, 40), (6, 36), (5, 25), (4, 16) and (10, 50). Items are divisible. What is the maximum total value that can be carried? (Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Sort by value per unit weight, take whole items in that order and split the first item that does not fit completely.
steps: Order: (6, 36) ratio 6, then the ratio-5 items (8, 40), (5, 25), (10, 50) in any order, then (4, 16) ratio 4.
Take (6, 36): weight 6, value 36, capacity left 14.
Take (8, 40): weight 14, value 76, capacity left 6.
Take (5, 25): weight 19, value 101, capacity left 1.
Take 1 of the 10 units of (10, 50): value 50 × (1/10) = 5, giving 106 with the knapsack exactly full.
solution.trap: Ignoring the fractional tail and answering 101, the value of the whole items only. In this instance starting from the highest-value item (10, 50) also happens to reach 106, which can hide a wrong method: value order is not optimal in general, ratio order is.

questions.question: A 0/1 knapsack has capacity 10 and three items given as (weight, value): (6, 30), (5, 20), (5, 20). The ratio-greedy algorithm takes items in decreasing order of value per unit weight and never splits an item. What value does it return, and what is the optimum?
options: Greedy 30, optimum 40
Greedy 30, optimum 45
Greedy 40, optimum 40
Greedy 46, optimum 40

solution.concept: On 0/1 knapsack the ratio rule can be forced to waste capacity, because the item that fills the remainder may be indivisible.
steps: Ratios: 30/6 = 5, and 20/5 = 4 for each of the other two items.
Greedy takes (6, 30): weight 6, value 30, capacity left 4.
Neither remaining item of weight 5 fits, so greedy stops at value 30.
The optimal solution takes both (5, 20) items: weight 10, value 40.
So greedy gives 30 and the optimum is 40 — a gap of 10 on a three-item instance.
solution.trap: Answering 46 by allowing a split of the second item. That is the fractional answer (30 + 20 × 4/5 = 46) and is not available in 0/1 knapsack.

questions.question: The optimality of ratio-greedy for fractional knapsack is proved by an exchange argument. Which one of the following is the essential step of that proof?
options: Sort the items by weight and show that any solution which uses a heavier item before a lighter one can be improved.

Take an optimal solution that agrees with greedy on the longest possible prefix; if it differs at the next item x, move weight from the lowest-ratio item that the solution uses to x, which keeps the total weight and cannot decrease the value, so an optimal solution agreeing on one more item exists.
Show by induction on the capacity that the greedy first choice is the unique optimal first choice.
Show that the linear-programming relaxation of fractional knapsack has an integral optimum, so greedy and the optimum coincide.

solution.concept: An exchange argument replaces part of an optimal solution by the greedy choice without losing optimality, so that an optimal solution containing the greedy choice exists; induction then finishes the proof.
steps: Let G be the greedy solution and O an optimal solution agreeing with G on the longest prefix of items.
At the first disagreement the greedy item x has ratio at least that of every item still used by O after the prefix, because greedy took items in non-increasing ratio order.
Move weight δ from the lowest-ratio item y that O still uses to x, where δ is the amount of x that greedy takes and that O does not.
Total weight is unchanged, so feasibility is preserved; the change in value is δ (v_x/w_x - v_y/w_y) ≥ 0, so O does not become worse.
Repeating the exchange gives an optimal solution equal to G, so G is optimal.
Option (A) sorts by weight, which is irrelevant; option (C) is false because the greedy first choice need not be unique; option (D) is false because the LP optimum is generally fractional.
solution.trap: Thinking the greedy choice must be unique. Ties in ratio give several optimal first choices, and the proof only needs one optimal solution containing the greedy choice, not uniqueness.

questions.question: An item weighs 12 kg and is worth ₹180 in total. In the fractional-knapsack greedy rule, what is this item's value per unit weight? (Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: The greedy key of an item is its value density v_i/w_i — value per single unit of weight.
steps: Value = 180, weight = 12.
Density = 180 / 12 = 15 value units per kg.
This density, not the total value 180, is what the greedy sort compares between items.
solution.trap: Sorting by total value instead of density. A heavy item can have a large total value and still be a poor use of capacity.

questions.question: Huffman's algorithm repeatedly removes the two smallest frequencies, merges them and inserts the sum. With a binary min-heap, what is the running time for n symbols?
options: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n²)
O(2ⁿ)

solution.concept: There are n-1 merges and each merge performs a constant number of heap operations, each costing O( log n).
steps: Build the heap from n frequencies: O(n) with bottom-up heapify.
Perform n-1 merges; each does two extractions and one insertion, i.e. three heap operations of cost O( log n).
Total O(n) + O(n log n) = O(n log n).
A sorted-list implementation gives the same bound; the naive O(n²) scan for the two minima is what the heap replaces.
solution.trap: Assuming sorting is required first. Sorting is one valid route, but the heap alone already achieves O(n log n) and needs no pre-sorted input.

questions.question: Six symbols have frequencies 5, 9, 12, 13, 16 and 45. For a Huffman tree on these frequencies, what is the total cost — the sum of all merged weights, which equals the weighted external path length?

solution.concept: Each merge adds the merged weight to the total cost, and the sum of merge costs equals Σ_i f_i · ℓ_i, the weighted external path length of the Huffman tree.
steps: Merge 5 and 9 → 14. Cost so far 14. Heap: 12, 13, 14, 16, 45.
Merge 12 and 13 → 25. Cost 39. Heap: 14, 16, 25, 45.
Merge 14 and 16 → 30. Cost 69. Heap: 25, 30, 45.
Merge 25 and 30 → 55. Cost 124. Heap: 45, 55.
Merge 45 and 55 → 100. Cost 224.
solution.trap: Reporting 100, the root weight, or the sum of the original frequencies. The cost is the sum of every merge, because a symbol merged early is paid for again at each level above it.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about Huffman coding are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Every Huffman code is prefix-free.
For a fixed multiset of symbol frequencies, Huffman's algorithm produces a code of minimum expected codeword length.
For a fixed multiset of symbol frequencies, the Huffman tree is unique.
Two symbols of equal frequency may be exchanged in a Huffman tree without changing the total cost.
Adding one more symbol of positive frequency to the alphabet can never increase the average codeword length.

solution.concept: Huffman codes are built on a full binary tree, so no codeword is a prefix of another, and the greedy merge of the two smallest weights is optimal for the weighted external path length.
steps: (A) is true: codewords are root-to-leaf paths, and a leaf has no leaf below it.
(B) is the optimality theorem for Huffman coding.
(C) is false: ties produce different but equally optimal trees — for frequencies 1, 1, 2 either pair of equal-frequency symbols may be merged first.
(D) is true: swapping two equal-frequency leaves changes no leaf depth times frequency, so the cost is unchanged.
(E) is false: a new symbol must be given a codeword, which lengthens some existing codewords and increases the average length.
solution.trap: Reading 'minimum expected length' as 'the code is unique'. Optimality is a property of the cost, not of the tree; Huffman trees are optimal but frequently not unique.

questions.question: Five symbols have frequencies 1, 1, 2, 3 and 5. What is the total cost of Huffman's tree on these frequencies, that is, the sum of all merged weights? (Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Sum the weights produced by each merge; the total is the weighted external path length of the Huffman tree.
steps: Merge 1 and 1 → 2. Cost 2. Heap: 2, 2, 3, 5.
Merge 2 and 2 → 4. Cost 6. Heap: 3, 4, 5.
Merge 3 and 4 → 7. Cost 13. Heap: 5, 7.
Merge 5 and 7 → 12. Cost 25.

Depth check on the resulting tree: the 5 sits at depth 1, the 3 at depth 2, the symbol of frequency 2 at depth 3, and the two symbols of frequency 1 at depth 4, so 5·1 + 3·2 + 2·3 + 1·4 + 1·4 = 25, matching the merge sum.
solution.trap: Adding the original frequencies (12) instead of the merge costs. Every internal node's weight is charged once, and a symbol merged early is charged again at every level above it.

questions.question: For n ≥ 2 symbols with positive frequencies, what is the largest possible length of a Huffman codeword?
options: ⌈ log_2 n ⌉
n
It is unbounded as the frequencies become more skewed.

solution.concept: A Huffman tree is a full binary tree, and in a full binary tree every level except possibly the last contains at least one leaf once the tree is built by successive merges of two smallest weights.
steps: Each merge reduces the number of trees in the forest by one, from n down to 1, so exactly n-1 merges occur and the tree has n leaves and n-1 internal nodes.

Take a deepest leaf at depth d. Each of the d internal nodes on its root-to-leaf path has a second child, and the subtree hanging from that child contains at least one leaf not on the path; these d leaves are distinct, and together with the deepest leaf itself they are d+1 distinct leaves.
Since the tree has only n leaves, d + 1 ≤ n, so d ≤ n - 1.
The bound is attained by Fibonacci-like frequencies such as 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, …, where each merge creates the next weight and the tree degenerates into a path.
The balanced value ⌈ log_2 n ⌉ is only a lower bound on the height, not the maximum, so option (A) is wrong.
solution.trap: Assuming Huffman trees are balanced. They are optimal for expected length, not for height, and highly skewed frequencies give very deep trees.

questions.question: In a Huffman tree built for n ≥ 2 symbols, which statement about the internal nodes is TRUE?
options: Every internal node has exactly two children.
An internal node may have exactly one child when a frequency is zero.
An internal node may have more than two children when several frequencies are equal.
There are no internal nodes when all frequencies are equal.

solution.concept: Huffman's algorithm builds the tree by merging exactly two trees at a time, so every internal node is the parent of exactly two nodes.
steps: Each step removes two roots from the forest and creates one new root with those two as children.
Therefore every internal node has exactly two children — the tree is a full binary tree.
A node with one child would be a redundant merge and would waste a bit in every codeword.
Equal frequencies change which nodes are paired, never the arity.
solution.trap: Confusing Huffman trees with general tries, where a node may have one child. Huffman's merges are always binary.

questions.question: To select the largest set of mutually compatible activities, which greedy rule is correct?
options: Repeatedly choose the compatible activity with the earliest start time.
Repeatedly choose the compatible activity with the shortest duration.
Repeatedly choose the compatible activity with the earliest finish time.
Repeatedly choose the compatible activity with the latest finish time.

solution.concept: Finishing early leaves the most room for the remaining activities, so earliest-finish is the greedy choice that an exchange argument can defend.
steps: Earliest finish time frees the resource sooner than any other choice, so the set of activities still available is as large as possible.
Exchange argument: if an optimal solution starts with some activity y while greedy picks x with f_x ≤ f_y, replacing y by x keeps the solution feasible and no smaller.
Shortest duration (B) can be defeated by one long early activity that blocks two short ones.
Earliest start (A) can pick an activity that runs until the very end of the schedule.
solution.trap: Choosing by shortest duration or earliest start. Neither leaves the maximum remaining room; only the finish time determines when the resource is free again.

questions.question: Eleven activities have the intervals (start, finish): (1, 4), (3, 5), (0, 6), (5, 7), (3, 9), (5, 9), (6, 10), (8, 11), (8, 12), (2, 14), (12, 16). Two activities are compatible when one finishes no later than the other starts. What is the maximum number of mutually compatible activities?

solution.concept: Run earliest-finish greedy: sort by finish time, take an activity whenever its start is at least the finish of the last one taken.
steps: Take (1, 4); last finish 4.
Next start ≥ 4: (5, 7); last finish 7.
Next start ≥ 7: (8, 11); last finish 11.
Next start ≥ 11: (12, 16); last finish 16.
Selected: (1, 4), (5, 7), (8, 11), (12, 16) — four activities. An exhaustive check of all subsets confirms that no five of the eleven are mutually compatible, so 4 is the maximum.
solution.trap: Counting activities that merely touch in time, or taking the shortest activities first — (3, 5) and (5, 7) then block (8, 11) and (12, 16) only if the choice is made badly. Trust the finish-time order.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the unweighted activity-selection problem are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Choosing the compatible activity with the earliest finish time is optimal.
Choosing the compatible activity with the shortest duration is optimal.
Choosing the compatible activity that starts earliest is optimal.
With all weights equal to 1, the earliest-finish greedy maximises the number of activities selected.
When two activities share the same finish time, every subset of activities must be examined.

solution.concept: The earliest-finish rule is exactly the greedy rule that an exchange argument proves optimal for maximising the count of compatible intervals.
steps: (A) and (D) say the same thing: with unit weights, maximising the number selected is the objective, and earliest finish is optimal for it.
(B) is false: one long early activity may block two short ones that overlap each other less favourably — shortest-duration can pick an activity that ends late.
(C) is false: an activity that starts earliest may run to the end of the day.
(E) is false: ties are harmless — any of the tied activities can be taken, since they all free the resource at the same time.
solution.trap: Assuming a tie needs a search. Ties on finish time are interchangeable for feasibility, so no branching is required.

questions.question: Five activities have the intervals [1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 4], [4, 5] and [5, 6], where an activity finishing at time t is compatible with one starting at time t. What is the maximum number of activities that can be selected? (Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Compatibility allows touching endpoints, so a chain of back-to-back intervals is fully compatible.
steps: Take [1, 2]; last finish 2. The next interval starts at 2, and 2 ≥ 2, so it is compatible.
The same holds at every step, so all five are selected.
No interval can be added beyond these five, since the set is already the whole collection.
solution.trap: Treating a finish time equal to a start time as a conflict, which yields 3 (only the odd-indexed intervals). The standard definition permits touching endpoints.

questions.question: In weighted interval scheduling each interval i has a weight w_i, and the goal is to maximise the total weight of a set of compatible intervals. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: The earliest-finish greedy remains optimal, because it maximises the number of intervals selected.
Earliest-finish greedy can be suboptimal, while a dynamic program over intervals sorted by finish time runs in O(n log n) and is optimal.
The problem is NP-hard, so no polynomial-time algorithm is known for it.
Sorting the intervals by decreasing weight and taking greedily is optimal.

solution.concept: Counting intervals and weighing them are different objectives; once weights differ, a locally cheap choice can block a far more valuable one, and the problem needs the optimal-substructure recurrence of dynamic programming.
steps: Counterexample: intervals (1, 4) with weight 200, (1, 2) with weight 60 and (3, 4) with weight 60. Earliest finish takes (1, 2) and then (3, 4), total 120, while (1, 4) alone is worth 200.
So no fixed greedy rule based on finish time is optimal in general.
Let p(j) be the last interval finishing before interval j starts. Then OPT(j) = max(w_j + OPT(p(j)), OPT(j-1)), computable left to right after sorting by finish time.
Each p(j) is found by binary search, giving O(n log n) overall.
The problem is polynomial, so (C) is false; sorting by weight (D) ignores compatibility entirely.
solution.trap: Assuming the unweighted greedy carries over. The exchange argument for earliest finish uses the count of intervals, which is meaningless once weights differ.

questions.question: Build one vertex per interval and join two vertices when the corresponding intervals overlap. The resulting graph is an interval graph. Selecting the largest set of mutually compatible activities is the same as:
options: finding a maximum independent set in an interval graph, which the earliest-finish greedy solves optimally in O(n log n)
finding a maximum clique in an interval graph, which the earliest-finish greedy solves optimally
finding a minimum vertex cover, which is NP-hard on interval graphs
colouring the interval graph, which always needs at least four colours

solution.concept: Compatible means non-overlapping, so a set of compatible intervals is an independent set in the overlap graph; maximising the count is a maximum independent set problem.
steps: Vertices are intervals; edges join overlapping pairs.
A set of pairwise non-overlapping intervals has no edges inside it, i.e. it is an independent set.
For interval graphs the maximum independent set equals the number of intervals in the earliest-finish greedy selection, computed in O(n log n) after sorting.
The maximum clique of an interval graph is the maximum number of intervals sharing a point, which is a different question.
Minimum vertex cover is polynomial on interval graphs by König-type duality with maximum matching, and colouring needs only as many colours as the maximum overlap depth.
solution.trap: Confusing 'no two chosen intervals overlap' with 'all chosen intervals overlap'. The former is an independent set; the latter, a clique, answers a different question.

questions.question: The optimal merge pattern for n sorted files is obtained by repeatedly merging:
options: the two largest files
the two smallest files
the largest file with the smallest file
any two files, chosen in input order

solution.concept: Each record in a file is moved once per merge in which its file takes part, so files merged early are charged repeatedly. Small files must therefore be merged first, exactly as small frequencies must be deepest in a Huffman tree.
steps: The total cost is the weighted external path length of the merge tree, with file sizes as weights.
Minimising that sum places the smallest weights deepest, which is achieved by merging the two smallest available files at every step.
Merging the two largest first (A) puts the biggest weights at the greatest depths and maximises the cost.
The mixed rule (C) and the input-order rule (D) are not optimal in general.
solution.trap: Merging in input order, which is what a naive two-way merge sort of the files does. That is correct but not cost-optimal.

questions.question: Five sorted files hold 5, 10, 20, 30 and 30 records. They are combined into one file by the optimal merge pattern. What is the minimum total number of record moves?

solution.concept: Merging two files of sizes a and b moves a+b records. The total is the sum of the merged sizes, i.e. the weighted external path length of the merge tree.
steps: Merge 5 and 10 → 15. Cost 15. Files: 15, 20, 30, 30.
Merge 15 and 20 → 35. Cost 50. Files: 30, 30, 35.
Merge 30 and 30 → 60. Cost 110. Files: 35, 60.
Merge 35 and 60 → 95. Cost 205.
solution.trap: Merging in the given order (5+10, then +20, then +30, then +30) gives 15 + 35 + 65 + 95 = 210, which is larger. Order matters.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the optimal merge pattern are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Repeatedly merging the two smallest files produces a minimum-cost pattern.
The total cost equals the weighted external path length of the merge tree.
Every merge tree for a given set of files is a full binary tree, each internal node having two children.
Every binary merge tree over the same n files has the same total cost.
If all file sizes are distinct, the optimal merge tree is unique.

solution.concept: Optimal merge patterns are Huffman coding in different clothes: the same greedy rule, the same cost function and the same full-binary-tree structure.
steps: (A) is the greedy rule, proved optimal by an exchange argument.
(B) is the definition: a file at depth d is copied once per level, so it contributes d × its size.
(C) holds because each merge combines exactly two files into one, so every internal node has two children.
(D) is false: merging 5, 10, 20, 30, 30 in input order costs 210 while the optimal pattern costs 205.

(E) is false even with distinct sizes: for sizes 2, 3, 4, 5 the first merge creates 5, which ties with the existing file of size 5, and pairing the 4 with either of them gives the same cost 5 + 9 + 14 = 28 with two different trees.
solution.trap: Equating 'distinct sizes' with 'unique tree'. Distinct sizes still allow a merged weight to tie an existing one, so several optimal trees can exist.

questions.question: Five sorted files hold 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 records. Using the optimal merge pattern, what is the minimum total number of record moves? (Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Merge the two smallest available files at each step and accumulate the merged size.
steps: Merge 2 and 3 → 5. Cost 5. Files: 4, 5, 5, 6.
Merge 4 and 5 → 9. Cost 14. Files: 5, 6, 9.
Merge 5 and 6 → 11. Cost 25. Files: 9, 11.
Merge 9 and 11 → 20. Cost 45.
solution.trap: Merging left to right (2+3, +4, +5, +6) gives 5 + 9 + 14 + 20 = 48, so the greedy order saves three moves.

questions.question: In an optimal merge pattern that combines n files into one, how many pairwise merge operations are performed in total?
options: n
n log_2 n

solution.concept: Each merge reduces the number of files by exactly one, and the process stops when one file remains.
steps: Start with n files.
Each merge replaces two files by one, so the count drops by one.
To go from n to 1 requires exactly n - 1 merges, whatever order is used.
The merge tree therefore has n leaves and n - 1 internal nodes.
solution.trap: Confusing the number of merges with the number of record moves. Merges are n-1; moves depend on the sizes and on the order chosen.

questions.question: Huffman coding and optimal merge patterns share one greedy structure. Which of the following statements about that shared structure are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Both repeatedly combine the two smallest weights, and the resulting tree is optimal for the corresponding cost.
Both are instances of constructing a full binary tree of minimum weighted external path length.
In both problems the greedy choice is justified by an exchange argument.
In both problems the resulting tree also minimises the maximum depth of any leaf.
Both require Ω(n²) time because every pair of weights must be examined.

solution.concept: Write each file size as a frequency and each merge as an internal node: the two problems become one — build a full binary tree minimising the sum over leaves of weight times depth.
steps: (A) is the shared greedy rule: two smallest weights are combined at each step.
(B) makes the identity precise: the objective in both cases is the weighted external path length of a full binary tree.
(C) is the standard proof technique: replace part of an optimal tree by the greedy merge without increasing the cost.
(D) is false: the optimal tree for skewed weights is a path of depth n-1, so it does not minimise height. Minimising height is a different objective and needs a balanced tree.
(E) is false: a min-heap gives O(n log n), and no pair enumeration is needed.
solution.trap: Assuming the optimal tree is balanced. Optimality here is about total cost, and the cheapest tree is often the most lopsided one.

questions.question: In the fractional knapsack problem the items are divisible. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: The problem is solved optimally in O(n log n) time by sorting the items on value per unit weight.
The problem needs dynamic programming, because a greedy choice may have to be undone later.
The problem is NP-hard, exactly like 0/1 knapsack.
The greedy algorithm may end up taking three or more items fractionally.

solution.concept: Fractional knapsack is a continuous problem: the exchange rate between weight and value is the ratio v_i/w_i, and only that ratio decides which item deserves the scarce capacity.
steps: Sorting on the ratio costs O(n log n) and filling the knapsack afterwards costs O(n), so the whole algorithm is O(n log n).
At most one item is split, because the first item that does not fit whole exhausts whatever capacity is left.
Divisibility is exactly what makes the exchange argument valid, so no dynamic program and no backtracking is needed.
0/1 knapsack is the NP-hard relative; the fractional version is polynomial and its greedy solution is optimal.
solution.trap: Options C and D are the usual slips: confusing the fractional problem with its NP-hard 0/1 cousin, and imagining that several items get cut. The split happens at most once, at the boundary item.

questions.question: A knapsack has capacity 18. The available items, given as (weight, value), are (6, 42), (9, 54), (4, 20) and (5, 25). Items are divisible. What is the maximum total value that can be carried? (Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Sort by value per unit weight in decreasing order, take whole items while they fit, then split the first item that does not fit.
steps: Order: (6, 42) with ratio 7, then (9, 54) with ratio 6, then the two ratio-5 items in either order.
Take (6, 42): weight 6, value 42, capacity left 12.
Take (9, 54): weight 15, value 96, capacity left 3.
Take 3 of the 4 units of (4, 20): value 20 × (3/4) = 15.
Total value 96 + 15 = 111, with the knapsack exactly full.
solution.trap: Answering 96 by taking only the whole items, or splitting (5, 25) first because it looks lighter. The ratio order — not the weight and not the total value — decides.

questions.question: A knapsack has capacity 12 and the divisible items (weight, value) are (5, 30), (4, 20), (6, 36) and (3, 15). The maximum total value the ratio-greedy algorithm carries is:

solution.concept: Take items in decreasing ratio order and split only the boundary item.
steps: The two ratio-6 items come first: (5, 30) and (6, 36).
Take (5, 30): weight 5, value 30, capacity left 7.
Take (6, 36): weight 11, value 66, capacity left 1.
Take 1 unit of a ratio-5 item: value 5. Total 66 + 5 = 71.
solution.trap: Answering 66 by stopping at the whole items, or 75 by using a capacity of 15. Check the fractional tail separately: 1 unit at ratio 5.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the fractional knapsack greedy algorithm are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: If every item has the same value per unit weight, then every order of the items gives an optimal solution.
If the total weight of all the items is at least the capacity, the greedy knapsack ends up completely full.
The algorithm takes a fraction of an item exactly when that item does not fit whole into the remaining capacity.
The algorithm may skip a high-ratio item in order to take two lower-ratio items whose total weight is larger.

solution.concept: With divisible items the objective is linear in the fraction taken, so value per unit weight is the only thing that matters.
steps: Option A: when all ratios are equal, any order fills the capacity with the same total value, so every order is optimal. True.
Option B: as long as the total weight reaches the capacity, the algorithm keeps taking whole items and then splits one, so the knapsack is exactly full. True.
Option C: whole items are taken while they fit; the first item that does not fit is split. True.
Option D: skipping a higher-ratio item for lower-ratio ones strictly lowers the value per unit of capacity, so it can never be optimal. False.
solution.trap: Option D describes what 0/1 knapsack does — leaving capacity unused — and candidates carry that habit over. With divisible items the knapsack is always filled, so there is no reason to prefer a lower ratio.

questions.question: A knapsack has capacity 25 and the divisible items (10, 60), (8, 48), (7, 35), (5, 30) and (12, 72). The maximum total value that can be carried is:

solution.concept: Ratio order decides; ties in the ratio are harmless, but a lower-ratio item must never be preferred for the leftover capacity.
steps: Four items tie at ratio 6 and one sits at ratio 5.
Take (10, 60): weight 10, value 60, capacity left 15.
Take (8, 48): weight 18, value 108, capacity left 7.
Take (5, 30): weight 23, value 138, capacity left 2.
Take 2 units of (12, 72) at ratio 6: value 12. Total 138 + 12 = 150, knapsack exactly full.
solution.trap: 148 comes from taking the leftover 2 units out of (7, 35), simply because it is the next item in the list. Its ratio is 5, not 6, so it is the wrong item for the leftover capacity.

questions.question: A knapsack has capacity 11 and the divisible items (4, 24), (5, 25), (6, 30) and (2, 10). What is the maximum total value that can be carried? (Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Sort by value per unit weight, fill whole items, split the boundary item.
steps: Take (4, 24): weight 4, value 24, capacity left 7.
Take (5, 25): weight 9, value 49, capacity left 2.
Take 2 units of any ratio-5 item: value 10.
Total 49 + 10 = 59, knapsack exactly full.
solution.trap: Answering 54 by stopping at the whole items, or 60 by rounding the capacity up to 12. The fractional tail of 2 units is worth 10, not 5.

questions.question: Huffman's algorithm repeatedly merges the two smallest frequencies. Implemented with a binary min-heap, its running time for n symbols is:
options: O(n log n)
O(n)

solution.concept: A Huffman tree on n leaves has exactly n − 1 merges, and each merge performs two extractions and one insertion on the heap.
steps: There are n − 1 merges in total.
Each heap operation costs O(log n), and each merge performs three of them.
Total time O(n log n).
If the frequencies arrive already sorted, two FIFO queues replace the heap and the bound improves to O(n).
solution.trap: Option B comes from scanning an unsorted list for the two minima at every step, which is O(n) per merge. The heap, or the two-queue trick on sorted input, removes that factor.

questions.question: Four symbols have frequencies 2, 3, 4 and 5. What is the total cost of a Huffman tree on these frequencies — that is, the sum over symbols of frequency × codeword length? (Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: The cost of a Huffman tree equals the sum of the weights of all its merges, which is the same as the weighted external path length.
steps: Merge 2 and 3 into 5. Merge cost 5.
The queue now holds 4, 5 and the new 5.
Merge 4 and 5 into 9. Merge cost 9. Queue: 5, 9.
Merge 5 and 9 into 14. Merge cost 14.
Total cost 5 + 9 + 14 = 28.
solution.trap: Reporting only the final merge (14) or the sum of the original frequencies (14). The cost accumulates over every merge, not just the last one.

questions.question: Five symbols have frequencies 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. The total cost of a Huffman tree on these frequencies is:

solution.concept: Every merge inserts its own weight back into the queue, so a newly formed value competes with the original frequencies.
steps: Merge 1 and 2 into 3. Cost 3. Queue: 3, 3, 4, 5.
Merge 3 and 3 into 6. Cost 6. Queue: 4, 5, 6.
Merge 4 and 5 into 9. Cost 9. Queue: 6, 9.
Merge 6 and 9 into 15. Cost 15.
solution.trap: 32 comes from pairing 4 and 5 too early, or from forgetting to push the merged value back into the queue. After the first merge the value 3 must compete with the original 3, 4 and 5.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about Huffman coding are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: For a given frequency distribution, Huffman's algorithm produces a prefix code of minimum expected codeword length.
The Huffman code for a given frequency distribution is unique.
Every full binary tree with n leaves defines a prefix code for n symbols.
In a Huffman tree no codeword is a prefix of another codeword.

solution.concept: Reading the root-to-leaf paths of a full binary tree as codewords gives a prefix-free code; Huffman's merge rule makes that code optimal for the given frequencies.
steps: Option A: Huffman's optimality is proved by the sibling and exchange arguments, so its expected length is minimal. True.
Option B: ties between equal frequencies, and the freedom to place either child on the left, produce several different optimal trees. False.
Option C: leaves are at distinct nodes of a binary tree, so no root-to-leaf path is a prefix of another. True.
Option D: codewords end at leaves, and no leaf is an ancestor of another leaf. True.
solution.trap: Option B is the standard trap: an optimal code is not the optimal code. With ties — and there are ties in almost every real distribution — several distinct Huffman trees have the same minimal cost.

questions.question: Six symbols each have frequency 1. In a Huffman tree built on these frequencies, the length of the longest codeword is:

solution.concept: Equal frequencies make Huffman behave like a balanced merge: each round pairs up the smallest values, and the tree depth is governed by how many rounds are needed.
steps: Merge 1 + 1 = 2. Queue: 1, 1, 2, 2.
Merge 1 + 1 = 2. Queue: 2, 2, 2.
Merge 2 + 2 = 4. Queue: 2, 4.
Merge 2 + 4 = 6. Total merge cost 2 + 2 + 2 + 4 + 6 = 16.
Leaf depths: the two symbols merged in the last step sit at depth 1 and 2, and the four symbols under the weight-4 subtree sit at depths 2 and 3.
So two codewords have length 2 and four have length 3; the longest codeword has length 3.
solution.trap: Assuming the answer is always ⌈log2 6⌉ = 3 for the wrong reason. Huffman guarantees nothing about balance in general — with frequencies 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 a tree of depth up to 5 is possible for other merge orders, and the bound is n − 1, not log n.

questions.question: Six symbols have frequencies 5, 7, 10, 15, 20 and 45. What is the total cost of a Huffman tree on these frequencies? (Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Repeatedly merge the two smallest current values and add the merged value to the running cost.
steps: Merge 5 and 7 into 12. Cost 12. Queue: 10, 12, 15, 20, 45.
Merge 10 and 12 into 22. Cost 22. Queue: 15, 20, 22, 45.
Merge 15 and 20 into 35. Cost 35. Queue: 22, 35, 45.
Merge 22 and 35 into 57. Cost 57. Queue: 45, 57.
Merge 45 and 57 into 102. Cost 102.
solution.trap: Re-sorting the original frequencies at every step instead of inserting the merged value. After the first merge the value 12 has to compete with 10, and missing that changes every later merge.

questions.question: To select the largest set of mutually compatible activities, the correct greedy rule is to:
options: sort the activities by finishing time and repeatedly take the next activity that starts no earlier than the last chosen one finishes.
sort the activities by starting time and take them in that order.
always take the activity of shortest duration first.
always take the activity that starts earliest and finishes latest.

solution.concept: Finishing as early as possible leaves the largest remaining window, so the earliest-finish choice is safe: some optimal solution contains it.
steps: Exchange argument: let a be the activity of earliest finish in a compatible set that also starts after the current time. Any optimal solution can swap its first activity for a without losing compatibility, because a finishes no later.
Repeating the swap proves the greedy choice is optimal at every step.
Sorting by start time fails: an early-starting, long activity blocks many others.
Shortest duration fails: a short activity in the middle of the day can straddle two others.
Taking the earliest start with the latest finish is the worst of the four.
solution.trap: Shortest-duration-first feels efficient and is wrong: duration says nothing about how much of the timeline is consumed at the edges. Only the finish time bounds the remaining schedule.

questions.question: Five activities have the intervals (start, finish) (1, 3), (2, 4), (3, 5), (5, 6) and (4, 7). Activities that touch at an endpoint are compatible. What is the maximum number of mutually compatible activities?

solution.concept: Sort by finishing time, then sweep left to right taking every activity whose start is at least the finish of the last one taken.
steps: Take (1, 3). Last finish is 3.
Next with start ≥ 3: (3, 5). Last finish is 5.
Next with start ≥ 5: (5, 6). Last finish is 6.
(4, 7) starts at 4, which is before 6, so it is rejected.
Three activities: (1, 3), (3, 5), (5, 6).
solution.trap: Answering 2 by taking (1, 3) and then (4, 7) — a valid set, but not a maximum one. The endpoint rule also matters: (3, 5) is compatible with (1, 3) only because touching at 3 is allowed.

questions.question: Five activities have the intervals (0, 5), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4) and (4, 6). Activities that touch at an endpoint are compatible. The maximum number of mutually compatible activities is:

solution.concept: The earliest-finish sweep never needs to look back, so one pass after sorting is enough.
steps: Take (1, 2); last finish 2.
Take (2, 3); last finish 3.
Take (3, 4); last finish 4.
Take (4, 6); last finish 6. The long activity (0, 5) is skipped.
Four activities in total.
solution.trap: Taking (0, 5) first because it is listed first, which leaves room for only two more. Listing order is irrelevant — the finish time is what the algorithm sorts on.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the unweighted activity-selection problem are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Choosing the activity that finishes earliest leaves the maximum possible room for the remaining activities.
Choosing the activity of shortest duration first is optimal.
The running time of the greedy algorithm is dominated by the sorting step, O(n log n).
After an activity is chosen, only activities that start at or after its finishing time are considered.

solution.concept: The greedy-choice property holds for the earliest-finish rule, and the rest of the algorithm is a single linear sweep after sorting.
steps: Option A: an earlier finish can only enlarge the set of compatible successors, so it is always at least as good. True.
Option B: a short activity placed in the middle of the timeline can overlap two others. False.
Option C: sorting costs O(n log n); the sweep costs O(n). True.
Option D: compatibility is defined by start ≥ last finish, so that is exactly the filter used. True.
solution.trap: Option B is tempting because 'short' sounds like 'leaves more room', but duration measures length, not the position of the left edge. Only the finish time bounds what can follow.

questions.question: In weighted interval scheduling each interval carries a weight and the goal is to maximise the total weight of a compatible set. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: The earliest-finish greedy rule remains optimal once weights are added.
A dynamic program over the intervals sorted by finish time, with a binary search for the last compatible interval, solves the problem in O(n log n) time.
The problem is NP-hard for arbitrary positive weights.
Sorting by weight and taking intervals greedily is optimal, because all weights are positive.

solution.concept: Adding weights destroys the greedy-choice property: a single heavy interval can be worth more than several light compatible ones, so the choice must be optimised rather than fixed.
steps: Option A: one long heavy interval can beat three short light ones, so earliest finish is no longer safe. False.

Option B: with intervals sorted by finish, let p(j) be the last interval compatible with j, found by binary search. Then OPT(j) = max(w_j + OPT(p(j)), OPT(j − 1)), giving O(n log n) after sorting. True.
Option C: the DP is polynomial, so the problem is not NP-hard. False.
Option D: a very heavy interval that blocks two moderately heavy ones defeats any weight-order rule. False.
solution.trap: Option A is the most common error: candidates learn activity selection as a greedy problem and assume weights are a detail. The weight is precisely what breaks the exchange argument.

questions.question: Six activities have the intervals (1, 4), (2, 3), (3, 5), (6, 7), (5, 8) and (8, 9). Activities that touch at an endpoint are compatible. The maximum number of mutually compatible activities is:

solution.concept: Sort by finish and sweep, keeping the last finish time.
steps: Take (2, 3); last finish 3.
Next start ≥ 3: (3, 5); last finish 5.
Next start ≥ 5: (6, 7) — it finishes before (5, 8), so it comes first; last finish 7.
Next start ≥ 7: (8, 9); last finish 9.
solution.trap: Stopping at 3 by taking (1, 4) or (5, 8). (6, 7) fits inside (5, 8), so choosing the shorter, earlier-finishing interval keeps (8, 9) available as well.

questions.question: Build the interval graph of a set of activities: one vertex per activity, with an edge between two activities that overlap. Which quantity equals the minimum number of rooms needed to run every activity without a clash?
options: the chromatic number of the interval graph, which equals its maximum clique — the largest number of activities overlapping at any single instant
the size of a maximum independent set of the interval graph
the number of activities minus the size of a maximum independent set
the number of activities

solution.concept: Interval graphs are perfect, so the chromatic number equals the clique number; the clique number is the peak overlap.
steps: A colouring assigns rooms so that overlapping activities get different colours.
The clique number is the maximum number of activities sharing a common instant, and those all need different rooms, so χ ≥ ω.
Interval graphs are perfect, so χ = ω: scheduling in peak-overlap many rooms always works.
The maximum independent set is the largest set of mutually compatible activities — the activity-selection answer, not the number of rooms.
solution.trap: Option B is the activity-selection answer dressed up as a colouring question. A maximum independent set says how many activities can share one room, not how many rooms are needed.

questions.question: The optimal merge pattern for n sorted files is obtained by repeatedly merging:
options: the two files of smallest current size
the two files of largest current size
the first two files in the order given
the smallest file with the largest file

solution.concept: This is Huffman's rule applied to file sizes: every record in a file pays one move for each merge the file takes part in, so small files should be merged often and large files rarely.
steps: Total cost is the weighted external path length of the merge tree.
Deep leaves are merged more often, so they must be the cheapest files.
Hence the two smallest current sizes are merged first, and the result re-enters the pool.
The number of merges is fixed at n − 1; only their costs can be controlled.
solution.trap: Option B maximises rather than minimises the cost — it is the classic 'wrong direction' distractor. Option C is what a naive left-to-right merge does and is generally not optimal.

questions.question: Five sorted files hold 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12 records. Using the optimal merge pattern, what is the minimum total number of record moves needed to combine them into one file? (Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Repeatedly merge the two smallest files; the total cost is the sum of all merge costs, which equals the weighted external path length.
steps: Merge 4 and 6 into 10. Cost 10. Pool: 8, 10, 10, 12.
Merge 8 and 10 into 18. Cost 18. Pool: 10, 12, 18.
Merge 10 and 12 into 22. Cost 22. Pool: 18, 22.
Merge 18 and 22 into 40. Cost 40.
solution.trap: Merging left to right gives 10 + 18 + 28 + 40 = 96, which is not optimal. Also, the answer is the sum of the merge costs, not the size of the final file (40).

questions.question: Four sorted files hold 1, 2, 3 and 4 records. The minimum total number of record moves needed to merge them into one file is:

solution.concept: Merge the two smallest current files each time and accumulate every merge cost.
steps: Merge 1 and 2 into 3. Cost 3. Pool: 3, 3, 4.
Merge 3 and 3 into 6. Cost 6. Pool: 4, 6.
Merge 4 and 6 into 10. Cost 10.
solution.trap: Merging any other pair first costs more: starting with 2 + 3 = 5 gives 5 + 5 + 10 = 20, and starting with 3 + 4 = 7 gives 7 + 3 + 10 = 20. Only the two-smallest rule reaches 19.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the optimal merge pattern are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: It minimises the total number of record moves needed to combine all the files.
It is produced by repeatedly merging the two files of smallest current size.
Its total cost equals the sum, over all files, of file size × depth of that file in the merge tree.
Merging the two largest files first minimises the total number of record moves.

solution.concept: The merge process is exactly Huffman's algorithm on the file sizes, and its cost is the weighted external path length of the resulting full binary tree.
steps: Option A: that is the objective the pattern is defined to minimise. True.
Option B: the two-smallest rule is Huffman's rule, and Huffman's tree is optimal. True.
Option C: a file at depth d takes part in d merges and pays its size once per merge, so the total is Σ size × depth. True.
Option D: putting the largest files at the greatest depth maximises the cost, the opposite of what is wanted. False.
solution.trap: Option D is the mirror-image error. Deep positions are expensive, so they must be filled by the smallest files; putting the largest files deepest is precisely what the algorithm avoids.

questions.question: An optimal merge pattern combines n files into one. Which of the following statements about its merge tree are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: The tree is a full binary tree with n leaves and n − 1 internal nodes.
Exactly n − 1 pairwise merge operations are performed.
The largest file always ends up at depth 1 in the tree.
The total number of record moves equals the weighted external path length of the merge tree.

solution.concept: Each merge replaces two nodes by their parent, so the tree is full and has n − 1 internal nodes; the cost is the weighted external path length.
steps: Option A: every internal node has exactly two children and there are n leaves, so the internal count is n − 1. True.
Option B: each merge creates one internal node, and there are n − 1 of them. True.
Option C: a file sits at depth 1 only when n = 2. For n ≥ 3 the largest file is at the shallowest depth, which is at least 2. False.
Option D: a file at depth d is copied once per merge along its path, so the total is Σ size × depth. True.
solution.trap: Option C confuses 'shallowest' with 'depth 1'. The largest file is merged last, so it is the child of the root only when there are just two files.

questions.question: Six sorted files hold 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 and 13 records. The minimum total number of record moves needed to merge them into one file is:

solution.concept: Take the two smallest current sizes at every step and accumulate the merge costs.
steps: Merge 3 and 5 into 8. Cost 8. Pool: 7, 8, 9, 11, 13.
Merge 7 and 8 into 15. Cost 15. Pool: 9, 11, 13, 15.
Merge 9 and 11 into 20. Cost 20. Pool: 13, 15, 20.
Merge 13 and 15 into 28. Cost 28. Pool: 20, 28.
Merge 20 and 28 into 48. Cost 48.
solution.trap: 120 comes from merging 9 and 13 instead of 9 and 11 at the third step — a single mis-step at any stage changes the total. Re-check that the pool is re-sorted after every merge.

questions.question: The matrix-chain problem multiplies n matrices A₁ A₂ … Aₙ. In the dynamic-programming solution, how many distinct subproblems m[i][j] (with 1 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ n) does the table hold?
options: n²
2ⁿ

solution.concept: The DP state is an interval of the chain: m[i][j] is the minimum number of scalar multiplications needed to compute the product Aᵢ Aᵢ₊₁ … Aⱼ. The state is identified by the two end indices, and the end indices satisfy i ≤ j.
steps: Every subproblem is a pair (i, j) with 1 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ n.
For a fixed i, the possible j are i, i+1, …, n, which is n − i + 1 choices.
Summing over i = 1 … n gives n + (n−1) + … + 1 = n(n+1)/2.
The diagonal i = j (a single matrix, cost 0) is part of the table: it is the base case the recurrence builds on.
solution.trap: n² counts ordered pairs, and (n−1)² or n(n−1)/2 drops the diagonal. The diagonal is needed: m[i][i] = 0 is the base case without which the recurrence has no bottom.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The DP state is an interval of the chain: m[i][j] is the minimum number of scalar multiplications needed to compute the product Aᵢ Aᵢ₊₁ … Aⱼ. The state is identified by the two end indices, and the end indices satisfy i ≤ j.

Step by step.

  1. Every subproblem is a pair (i, j) with 1 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ n.
  2. For a fixed i, the possible j are i, i+1, …, n, which is n − i + 1 choices.
  3. Summing over i = 1 … n gives n + (n−1) + … + 1 = n(n+1)/2.
  4. The diagonal i = j (a single matrix, cost 0) is part of the table: it is the base case the recurrence builds on.

Answer: n(n+1)/2 subproblems — option (A).

Common misconception. n² counts ordered pairs, and (n−1)² or n(n−1)/2 drops the diagonal. The diagonal is needed: m[i][i] = 0 is the base case without which the recurrence has no bottom.

questions.question: Three matrices are given: A₁ is 10 × 20, A₂ is 20 × 30 and A₃ is 30 × 40. What is the minimum number of scalar multiplications needed to form A₁A₂A₃?

solution.concept: A parenthesisation fixes the order of multiplication, and the cost of multiplying a p×q matrix by a q×r matrix is p·q·r scalar multiplications. The dimensions of an intermediate product are the outer dimensions of the two operands.
steps: Option 1, (A₁A₂)A₃: A₁A₂ costs 10·20·30 = 6000 and yields a 10×30 matrix. Multiplying that by A₃ (30×40) costs 10·30·40 = 12 000. Total 18 000.
Option 2, A₁(A₂A₃): A₂A₃ costs 20·30·40 = 24 000 and yields a 20×40 matrix. Multiplying A₁ (10×20) by it costs 10·20·40 = 8000. Total 32 000.
The minimum is min(18 000, 32 000) = 18 000.
