solution.trap: 24 000 is only the cost of A₂A₃, a partial cost. 32 000 is the other parenthesisation; 38 000 comes from adding 24 000 and 14 000 of nothing in particular. Multiply only the three relevant dimensions at each step and add the two step costs.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A parenthesisation fixes the order of multiplication, and the cost of multiplying a p×q matrix by a q×r matrix is p·q·r scalar multiplications. The dimensions of an intermediate product are the outer dimensions of the two operands.

Step by step.

  1. Option 1, (A₁A₂)A₃: A₁A₂ costs 10·20·30 = 6000 and yields a 10×30 matrix. Multiplying that by A₃ (30×40) costs 10·30·40 = 12 000. Total 18 000.

questions.question: What is the length of a longest common subsequence of X = TRANSFER and Y = REFERENT?

solution.concept: A subsequence keeps the original order but may skip symbols. The LCS length is the value c[m][n] of the DP table c[i][j] = length of the LCS of the first i symbols of X and the first j symbols of Y.

solution.trap: 5 and 6 come from counting matching letters without regard to order, or from looking for a common substring. TRANSFER and REFERENT share many letters, but a subsequence must respect position order in both strings.

questions.question: What is the length of the longest palindromic subsequence of the string CHARACTER?

solution.concept: A longest palindromic subsequence of s is exactly a longest common subsequence of s and its reverse: a palindrome read backwards is itself, so any common subsequence of s and reverse(s) is a palindromic subsequence of s, and conversely.

The subsequence C-A-R-A-C is palindromic and appears in s at positions 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, so the length is at least 5.
Running the LCS DP on s and reverse(s) gives 5, so no palindromic subsequence of length 6 exists.
Answer: 5, from CARAC.

options: If x_m = y_n, then some longest common subsequence of X and Y ends with that common symbol.
If x_m ≠ y_n and c[m−1][n] ≥ c[m][n−1], then some longest common subsequence of X and Y is a longest common subsequence of X[1..m−1] and Y.
Every longest common subsequence of X and Y is a substring of both X and Y.
If X is a subsequence of Y, then the LCS length of X and Y is |X|.

solution.concept: The three structural lemmas behind the LCS recurrence: matching last symbols can be taken, mismatching last symbols can be dropped from one side, and the LCS of two strings one of which contains the other is the shorter string.
steps: (A) TRUE. If x_m = y_n, take an LCS of X[1..m−1] and Y[1..n−1] and append x_m: the result has length c[m−1][n−1] + 1 = c[m][n], which is optimal, so an optimal LCS ending in that symbol exists.

(C) FALSE. Subsequence is not substring: in X = TRANSFER and Y = REFERENT the LCS RFER is not contiguous in either string. Contiguity would make this the longest common substring problem, a different (and smaller-valued) quantity.
(D) TRUE. If every symbol of X appears in Y in order, X itself is a common subsequence of length |X|, and no common subsequence can exceed the shorter length, so the LCS length is exactly |X|.

  1. (A) TRUE. If x_m = y_n, take an LCS of X[1..m−1] and Y[1..n−1] and append x_m: the result has length c[m−1][n−1] + 1 = c[m][n], which is optimal, so an optimal LCS ending in that symbol exists.
  2. (B) TRUE. When x_m ≠ y_n the recurrence gives c[m][n] = max(c[m−1][n], c[m][n−1]); if the left term is the larger, an LCS of X[1..m−1] and Y of that length is also an LCS of X and Y, since appending x_m cannot help.
  3. (C) FALSE. Subsequence is not substring: in X = TRANSFER and Y = REFERENT the LCS RFER is not contiguous in either string. Contiguity would make this the longest common substring problem, a different (and smaller-valued) quantity.
  4. (D) TRUE. If every symbol of X appears in Y in order, X itself is a common subsequence of length |X|, and no common subsequence can exceed the shorter length, so the LCS length is exactly |X|.

(C) is the trap for candidates who have also met the longest common substring problem; the DP recurrence for the two is different (a substring DP resets to 0 on mismatch, while the LCS DP takes a maximum). (B) is easy to over-generalise: it holds only for the larger of the two terms.

questions.question: Which statement about the Floyd–Warshall algorithm is TRUE?
options: It runs in Θ(n³) time and is correct with negative edge weights as long as no negative-weight cycle is reachable.
It runs in Θ(n²) time on a dense graph.
It requires every edge weight to be non-negative.
It is a greedy algorithm, so it fails whenever an edge has negative weight.

solution.concept: Floyd–Warshall is a dynamic program over the set of allowed intermediate vertices; it never commits to a locally cheapest edge, so negative edge weights are harmless. What it cannot survive is a negative-weight cycle, because then shortest paths are undefined.
steps: Three nested loops over k (intermediate vertex), i and j give Θ(n³) time on an n-vertex graph.
The recurrence d^(k)[i][j] = min(d^(k−1)[i][j], d^(k−1)[i][k] + d^(k−1)[k][j]) only adds and compares path lengths; negative values are handled correctly.
A negative cycle shows up as some d[i][i] < 0 after the last iteration, which is how the algorithm detects it rather than silently failing.
Dijkstra is the greedy algorithm that requires non-negative weights; Floyd–Warshall is not Dijkstra.
solution.trap: Option (D) confuses Floyd–Warshall with Dijkstra. The greedy requirement (non-negative weights) belongs to Dijkstra; the DP requirement is the absence of a negative-weight cycle.

Vertex k must be an endpoint of the path.

Taking the minimum of the two cases gives the recurrence.
After k = n, every vertex is allowed as an intermediate, so d^(n)[i][j] is the true shortest-path distance.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the Floyd–Warshall algorithm are TRUE?
options: Replacing min by logical OR and + by logical AND in the recurrence computes the transitive closure of the graph.
A negative-weight cycle exists if and only if some d[i][i] < 0 after the final iteration.
The dynamic program is correct only if the graph is strongly connected.
d^(k)[i][j] is the length of a shortest i→j path all of whose intermediate vertices lie in {1, …, k}.

questions.question: A directed graph has vertices A, B, C, D and weighted edges A→B (3), A→C (8), B→C (2), B→D (5), C→D (1), D→A (2). The shortest-path distance from D to B is:

solution.concept: With a negative edge present, Dijkstra's greedy rule is unsafe, but Floyd–Warshall's DP is not: it compares complete path lengths rather than extending the cheapest prefix. The shortest path is found by allowing more intermediate vertices step by step.

Allow B as an intermediate: d[A][C] = min(4, d[A][B] + w(B,C)) = min(4, 3 − 2) = 1. The negative edge is now doing the work.
Allow D: d[A][E] = min(13, d[A][D] + 1) = min(13, 7) = 7.

options: On an unweighted graph, a breadth-first search from every vertex computes all-pairs distances faster than Floyd–Warshall.

If a negative-weight cycle is reachable, the final Floyd–Warshall matrix satisfies d[i][i] < 0 for every vertex i on that cycle.

steps: (A) TRUE. BFS from each vertex costs O(V·(V+E)), which on a sparse graph is far below Θ(V³); Floyd–Warshall ignores the sparsity.

(B) FALSE. Dijkstra finalises a vertex when it is popped, assuming no later path can be shorter. Take A→B (1), A→C (2), C→B (−2): Dijkstra from A pops B at distance 1 and finalises it, although the true distance is 0 through C. One negative edge is enough; no cycle is needed.

(C) TRUE. Bellman–Ford from a new source s with 0-weight edges to all vertices gives potentials h(v) = δ(s,v) satisfying w(u,v) + h(u) − h(v) ≥ 0. Reweighting preserves shortest paths, so V Dijkstra runs give O(V² log V + VE) with a binary heap.

(D) TRUE. A vertex i on a negative cycle can reach itself through that cycle with negative total weight, so d[i][i] < 0 after all vertices are allowed as intermediates; vertices not on the cycle keep d[i][i] = 0.
solution.trap: (B) is the persistent error: 'Dijkstra is fine as long as there is no negative cycle' is false — a single negative edge is enough to break it. (D) is often mis-stated as 'd[i][i] < 0 for all i', which would wrongly include vertices off the cycle.
